steps.body: Put mái after a verb to ask a yes/no question — it often works like an invitation ("...mái?" can mean "want to...?"). Answer "yes" by repeating the verb, or "no" by putting mâi in front of it.

steps.body: Use châi mái at the end of a statement when you already think something is true and just want to confirm it, like English "right?". Answer châi ("right") or mâi châi ("no, that's not right").
steps.title: Confirming with châi mái

steps.body: In Thai, brothers and sisters are always identified as either older or younger. Phîi is the prefix for "older" and nɔ́ɔng is for "younger". steps.title: Phîi and nɔ́ɔng

steps.body: Some relationship terms are used to refer to people you're not related to — in Thai culture everyone is considered a big family. Yaai and taa are used for a woman/man your grandmother's/grandfather's age (they literally refer to your mother's mother/father), and lung, pâa, and náa are used the same way for an uncle or aunt's age.
steps.title: One big family
